source.title: Understanding the robustness difference between stochastic gradient descent and adaptive gradient methods
source.authors: A. Ma; Yang-Chen Pan; Amir-massoud Farahmand

record.tranche_reason: The study compares standard test accuracy across optimizers and concludes that standard generalization differences are relatively small, refining the optimizer comparison in V4. Its perturbation-robustness results are outside the claim's scope.
record.gate_note: Only original test-set accuracy results bear on V4. Results under Gaussian noise and adversarial perturbations concern out-of-distribution robustness and are excluded. The paper reports Table 3 values as averages over three independently initialized and trained models; those averages are not separated into seed-level rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out image-classification accuracy across SGD, Adam and RMSProp using learning-rate selection with otherwise largely default optimizer settings. These results bear on V4 without requiring training accuracy or a train–test gap. Most reported comparisons show adaptive methods matching or outperforming SGD, qualifying the claimed optimizer penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly captures the authors' finding of relatively similar clean-test performance and substantially better perturbation robustness with SGD. Correct its added suggestion that V4 requires a train–test gap: V4 directly concerns held-out optimizer performance. The authors explain the robustness difference through target-irrelevant frequencies, synthetic linear-model dynamics and smaller Lipschitz upper bounds for SGD-trained networks.
record.recipe_differences: Compares SGD, Adam and RMSProp on original test accuracy and perturbation robustness; does not study random-label memorization or the claim's training–test error gap. Uses a wide learning-rate sweep and selects the model with highest validation accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported standard test accuracies vary by dataset and optimizer; the authors describe the overall standard-generalization difference as relatively small. Batch normalization and fine-tuned ViT are separate settings, but their reported robustness findings are outside this claim's scope.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD generally produces better Gaussian-noise and adversarial robustness than Adam and RMSProp despite similar clean-test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects robustness to input perturbations separately from clean-distribution generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD-trained networks have smaller computed Lipschitz upper bounds, and synthetic linear models can have similar standard risks but different adversarial risks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input sensitivity and the use of target-irrelevant features help explain optimizer-dependent robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing many low-energy or high-frequency DCT components from training inputs can preserve original-test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Substantial frequency information in training images can be dispensable for clean-test classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Speech Commands clean-test accuracies are 85.14% SGD, 85.47% Adam and 84.67% RMSProp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer differences in clean audio-classification accuracy can be small and vary in direction.

record.problems: Standard test accuracy is reported without corresponding training accuracy, so the train–test gap cannot be evaluated. Main comparisons average three trainings, and Table 3 gives no uncertainty estimates for those test values. The study focuses on robustness to perturbed inputs, which is outside the claim's scope.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible Table 3 original-test accuracy rows were left out. Perturbation accuracy, synthetic population-risk analyses, and Lipschitz estimates were excluded because they do not measure the natural-distribution training–test gap described in the versions. Table 6 optimizer-to-value assignment is unclear in the flattened text, so no numerical rows were reconstructed for it.

untested.parts: Paired random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

Language benchmarks; equal or better training performance; broader tuning beyond learning rates and the specified schedules; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers; word-level language models. No controlled comparison of tuning breadth is performed.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Controlled dropout comparisons and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing measures. Input sensitivity and Lipschitz bounds do not measure this claim.
Removal of examples selected by label memorization versus removal of random examples.

missing.what: All clean-test optimizer comparisons with batch normalization enabled: SGD/Adam/RMSProp accuracies are CIFAR10 92.24/93.38/93.57; CIFAR100 72.24/71.36/70.99; SVHN 94.16/96.62/96.44; Caltech101 78.61/79.58/75.56; Imagenette 89.35/91.88/91.93. These are eligible V4 results, not merely robustness findings.

Clean Imagenette accuracy for ViT-B/16 head fine-tuning: SGD 99.18%, Adam 99.93%, RMSProp 99.92%. Record the frozen encoder, Adam pretraining, 10 epochs, shared initial learning rate 0.01, cosine decay, warmup and batch size 512.

Momentum-SGD clean-test reference rows: CIFAR10 89.79%, CIFAR100 56.08%, SVHN 96.14%, Caltech101 69.89%, Imagenette 88.69%. Pair with the adaptive results in Table 3 to assess V4's momentum-SGD comparison.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4. Main image models use 200 epochs, learning-rate reductions at epochs 100 and 150, no weight decay, and a validation-selected learning rate; batch normalization is disabled unless specified. Numerical reversals describe reported means, not proven significant differences. Because V4 says adaptive methods often perform worse, these counterexamples qualify its scope rather than refute that frequency claim across benchmarks. Audio results were declared left out, so they are corrected under R28 rather than listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language benchmarks, training accuracy comparisons, broader optimizer tuning, decoupled weight decay, optimizer switching, and word-level language models.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test-accuracy changes.
